newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia 1997 budget will feel effects of donor cuts.
newsitem.headline: Zambia 1997 budget will feel effects of donor cuts.

text.p: Zambian Finance Minister Ronald Penza will be forced to cut spending and raise taxes in the face of donor cuts when he presents his 1997 budget on Friday, analysts said on Tuesday.

Western donors cut aid to Zambia last year after constitutional amendments by President Frederick Chiluba barred his main opponents from contesting a general election which he later won in a landslide.
Analysts told Reuters the Chiluba government will pay a price in the 1997 budget for this move and will be forced to raise taxes and cut spending.

"The donor component in the budget has always been substantial. Last year, for example, it accounted for over 35 percent of the budget and three quarters of capital expenditure. If it declines, the shortfall in revenue will be significant," said Griffins Nyirongo of the Economic Association of Zambia.
"The best way out may be for the government to opt for a deficit and hope that at some point, someone will come and fill it," he added.
Donor funds accounted for 421.6 billion kwacha ($320 million) of the 1,161.6 billion kwacha in the 1996 budget.
Of the 381.1 billion kwacha allocated to capital expenditure, 292.8 billion kwacha was provided by donors.
Most western governments, led by the United States, Britain, Germany, Sweden and Japan, say they will maintain the aid cuts through 1997.

Analysts say the government is likely to raise taxes to make up for reduced aid flows but warn that such measures would be disastrous for industry, just recovering from the initial shocks of structural adjustment.
"Increasing taxes would be catastrophic for industry," economic analyst Mark O'Donnel said.
"The government should improve its revenue collection, not raise taxes".
Zambia's industry is among the most heavily taxed in southern Africa with company tax at 30 percent, import duty ranging from 15 to 25 percent and value added tax at 20 percent.
Analysts believe the government will have to cut spending drastically if it is to manage the budget without donor aid inflows.
They propose that this be done in the non-productive sectors only.

"For example, the government undertook to reduce the staff at the ministry of agriculture from 7,000 to 5,000 three years ago. That has not been done. But those are the areas in which government can cut spending without hurting the economy," Zambia National Farmers Union chief George Gray said.
President Chiluba has said his government will have to cut spending in response to aid cuts, but did not identify the sectors which will be affected.
Addressing the national assembly recently, Chiluba said his government intended, anyway, to reduce its dependence on aid, starting this year.
But analysts doubt the government can manage a budget without significant donor inflows.
"The budget can not survive without donor aid," O'Donnel said.
"We were hoping for a budget to stimulate growth. However, we will be looking at a standstill budget, even a retrogressive budget," he added.
($=1,290 kwacha)
